The archive thus maintains the MOST LEARNABLE problems per niche at any given training stage.\n\n(f) **Solve-rate Recalibration and Emergent Curriculum.** After policy improvement, problems naturally shift to easier bins. A problem in 'hard number theory' (solve-rate 0.15) at step 100 may become 'medium number theory' (solve-rate 0.45) by step 300, vacating the hard cell and triggering new hard synthesis. This creates automatic difficulty escalation without explicit scheduling—a capability that SwS's static problem set fundamentally cannot provide.\n\n**Addressing the Sparse Policy Selection Challenge:**\nThe finding that RL affects only 1-3% of tokens (arXiv 2605.06241) does not undermine our approach. Following the 'Sharper Primitives' framework (arXiv 2602.08281), we reframe QD-RLVR's goal: comprehensive COVERAGE of latent reasoning primitives rather than capability creation. The MAP-Elites archive ensures systematic activation of primitives across all topic×difficulty combinations, sharpening precision across the full capability spectrum. Under this framing, archive diversity directly increases the range of high-entropy decision points where RL can provide useful signal. ## Overview

SwS (Self-aware Weakness-driven Problem Synthesis) is a framework that systematically identifies model deficiencies and leverages them for problem augmentation.

## Problem It Addresses

The paper focuses on Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), which has proven effective for training LLMs on complex reasoning tasks like mathematical problem solving, but requires high-quality problem sets with precise and verifiable answers. However, the scarcity of well-crafted human-labeled math problems and limited-verification answers in existing synthetic datasets limit their effectiveness. Additionally, most problem synthesis strategies indiscriminately expand the problem set without considering the model's capabilities, leading to low efficiency in generating useful questions.

## How SwS Works

The framework defines weaknesses as questions that the model consistently fails to learn through iterative sampling during RL training. It then extracts core concepts from these failure cases and synthesizes new problems to strengthen the model's weak areas in subsequent augmented training.

**Prism** is a question-centric self-evolution method introduced by Vaibhav Mishra that helps self-evolving reasoning frameworks (where LLMs improve their reasoning by iteratively generating and solving problems) avoid curriculum collapse.

Prior research showed that self-evolving systems can exhibit diversity collapse when posing new problems after just a few iterations, even when surface-level variation is preserved.

Prism addresses this by defining a persistent diversity signal over an embedding-induced semantic partition of mathematical problems and uses it to encourage balanced exploration of underrepresented regions across iterations. Prism also generated semantically diverse and challenging questions across iterations, resulting in the construction of the Prism-Math dataset comprising 100k mathematical questions.

## R-Diverse: Mitigating Diversity Illusion in Self-Play LLM Training

This paper presents a self-play framework that bootstraps LLM reasoning through an iterative Challenger–Solver loop, where the Challenger generates questions targeting the Solver's capabilities, and the Solver is optimized on generated data to expand its reasoning skills.

**The Problem:**
Existing frameworks like R-Zero often exhibit non-sustained improvement where early gains degrade as self-play continues, due to a key failure mode called Diversity Illusion—where the Solver's training signals appear diverse yet collapse into recurring underlying patterns.

**Two Types of Diversity Illusion:**
The paper identifies Local Diversity Illusion (diversity enforced only within-batch, inducing cross-iteration mode cycling) and Surface Diversity Illusion (where questions vary superficially but require near-identical reasoning skills).

**The Solution:**
R-Diverse proposes two aligned innovations: Memory-Augmented Penalty (MAP), which uses a persistent memory bank to discourage recycling across iterations, and Skill-Aware Measurement (SAM), which evaluates diversity by the reasoning skills exercised rather than surface variation of questions.

**Results:**
Across 10 math and general reasoning benchmarks, R-Diverse sustains gains over more iterations and consistently outperforms prior self-play methods.

Code is available at https://github.com/Gengsheng-Li/R-Diverse.

## Overview

CLPO (Curriculum-guided Learning for Policy Optimization) is a novel algorithm that creates a dynamic pedagogical feedback loop within the policy optimization process.

## Problem It Addresses

Recently, online Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become a key paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), but existing methods typically treat all training samples uniformly, overlooking the vast differences in problem difficulty relative to the model's current capabilities.

## Key Innovation

The core of CLPO leverages the model's own rollout performance to conduct real-time difficulty assessment, thereby constructing an Online Curriculum. This curriculum then guides an Adaptive Problem Restructuring mechanism, where the model acts as its own teacher: it diversifies medium-difficulty problems to promote generalization and simplifies challenging problems to make them more attainable.

## Results

CLPO achieves state-of-the-art performance across eight challenging mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks, with an average pass@1 improvement of 6.96% over other methods.

## Overview

VCRL is a curriculum reinforcement learning framework that dynamically controls the difficulty of training samples based on the variance of group rewards for improving LLMs on mathematical reasoning tasks.

## Key Problem and Insight

Existing rollout-based reinforcement learning methods (GRPO, DAPO, GSPO, etc.) fail to explicitly consider LLMs' learning ability for samples of different difficulty levels, which is contrary to the human cognitive process of mathematical reasoning tasks from easy to difficult.

The variance of the rollout group's reward partly reflects the difficulty of the current sample for LLMs, with samples that are too easy or too difficult having lower variance, while samples with moderate difficulty have higher variance.

## Methodology

VCRL strategically selects training samples based on high reward variance, interpreted as moderate difficulty, and integrates a replay memory for stable learning.

## Results

Experiments on five mathematical benchmarks and two models reveal the advantages of VCRL over the current LLM RL baselines. Evaluated on math benchmarks using Qwen3–4B/8B models, VCRL demonstrates significant improvements in performance and training stability.

## Vocabulary Dropout for Curriculum Diversity in LLM Co-Evolution

The paper is authored by Jacob Dineen and 3 other authors from Arizona State University and addresses co-evolutionary self-play, where one language model generates problems and another solves them, promising autonomous curriculum learning without human supervision.

### The Problem
In practice, the proposer quickly converges to a narrow distribution of problems that satisfy the reward function, and this diversity collapse renders the curriculum uninformative for the solver, stalling the co-evolutionary loop.

### The Solution
The paper introduces vocabulary dropout, a random mask applied to the proposer's output logits during both policy training and curriculum generation, as a lightweight mechanism to sustain diversity. The mask is hard and non-stationary, preventing the proposer from locking into fixed token sequences.

### Results
Training Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on mathematical reasoning via R-Zero, the authors found that vocabulary dropout sustains proposer diversity across lexical, semantic, and functional metrics throughout training, and yields solver improvements averaging +4.4 points at 8B, with the largest gains on competition-level benchmarks.

The paper was submitted to arXiv on April 3, 2026 (arXiv:2604.03472).

## COvolve: Adversarial Co-Evolution Framework

COvolve is a co-evolutionary framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to generate both environments and agent policies, expressed as executable Python code.

**Problem Addressed:**
A central challenge in building continually improving agents is that training environments are typically static or manually constructed, which restricts continual learning and generalization beyond the training distribution.

**Key Methodology:**
The framework models the interaction between environment and policy designers as a two-player zero-sum game, ensuring adversarial co-evolution in which environments expose policy weaknesses and policies adapt in response.

**Robustness Mechanism:**
To guarantee robustness and prevent forgetting as the curriculum progresses, the framework computes the mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium (MSNE) of the zero-sum game, thereby yielding a meta-policy.

**Outcomes:**
This process induces an automated curriculum in which environments and policies co-evolve toward increasing complexity. Experiments in urban driving, symbolic maze-solving, and geometric navigation showcase that COvolve produces progressively more complex environments.

The paper was authored by researchers from Örebro University's Machine Perception and Interaction Lab and was published on arXiv on March 30, 2026.

## Paper Overview

The paper "Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?" (arXiv:2504.13837) examines Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) and its effectiveness in enhancing reasoning performance of large language models, particularly on mathematics and programming tasks.

## Key Findings

The paper's surprising conclusion is that **RL does not truly incentivize new reasoning capacity beyond the base model**:

- The study finds that the current training setup does not elicit fundamentally new reasoning patterns.

- While RLVR-trained models outperform their base models at small k (e.g., k = 1), the base models achieve a higher pass@k score when k is large.

- All reasoning paths in the RLVR model are already present in the base model. For certain problems, RLVR training biases the distribution toward rewarded paths, improving sampling efficiency.

## Significance

This paper was a NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper Runner-Up. While RLVR significantly improves sampling efficiency (correct answers appear more often), it does not expand the model's fundamental reasoning capability boundary.

The research suggests that current RLVR techniques are best understood as inference-time optimization baked into weights, rather than a discovery engine for novel intelligence.

# CLPO Paper Analysis

**1) Problem Archive:**
No, CLPO does not maintain an archive. It works with the "DAPO-Math-17k dataset" during training and dynamically constructs batches from this single source.

**2) Online Problem Restructuring:**
Yes. CLPO "employs Adaptive Problem Restructuring (APR), a mechanism where the model acts as its own teacher to create more suitable learning materials." The system generates two types of restructured problems: diversified versions of medium-difficulty problems and simplified versions of hard problems, all created during training via language model prompts.

**3) Models and Sizes:**
The paper uses "Qwen3-8B" as the base model for all experiments. This is an 8-billion parameter language model.

**4) AIME Scores:**
Yes, reported as pass@1 metrics: AIME24 achieves 50.00% with CLPO, compared to 46.67% for the next-best baseline (DAPO and Critique-GRPO). The paper also reports "3.3% over the strongest baseline" on AIME2024.

**5) Online Curriculum Mechanism:**
The curriculum works via: (1) evaluating accuracy on each problem using multiple rollouts, (2) partitioning problems into hard/medium/easy based on thresholds (0.3, 0.7), (3) restructuring only medium and hard problems, and (4) filtering results to retain only samples with "0<Acc(q′,πθ)<1" for training.

**6) Publication Venue:**
The paper indicates future open-source release ("will open-source all our code") but doesn't specify a published venue. It appears to be an arXiv preprint (2509.25004).
